title: A Week of Diplomatic Choreography and Unresolved War: The UN General Assembly Closed Every Door It Opened
subhead: The 81st UN General Assembly framed a week in which the US and China extended a trade truce but solved nothing on Iran or Taiwan, Washington proposed the first trilateral Ukraine-Russia talks while Ukraine hit Moscow with its largest drone barrage of the war, and a US-Russia deal gutted UN safeguards on autonomous weapons. Meanwhile the Horn of Africa slid back toward a war that killed 600,000, and the Mecca Pact moved from declaration to military planning.

sections.heading: The Trump-Xi Summit: Warmth Without Substance, a Truce Without Trust
sections.body:
Xi Jinping's first Washington visit in over a decade began with a red carpet arrival at Joint Base Andrews — the first tarmac greeting by a US president since 1962 — and a B-1 bomber flyover. It ended with a state dinner whose guest list read like a tech-industry board meeting: OpenAI's Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Amazon's Jeff Bezos. Trump toasted a 'great friendship' and said the two had 'never gotten along better.'

The concrete deliverable was a trade truce extension to January, pushing back the previous November 10 expiry. Under the existing arrangement, Trump lowered tariff rates on some goods in exchange for Xi loosening restrictions on rare earth minerals. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two sides discussed whether a more substantive deal could follow. By week's end, Reuters reported a more specific figure: tariff cuts on $30 billion of goods in each direction, the clearest economic breakthrough of the visit.

But on every strategic question — Iran, Taiwan, AI — the summit produced no resolution. Xi urged Trump to oppose Taiwanese independence and handle the issue 'prudently,' per Xinhua, while the $14 billion Taiwan arms package remained an unresolved flashpoint. On Iran, Trump pressed Xi to cut support for Tehran and received assurances that China would not back Iran — a position consistent with Beijing's interest in stable Gulf oil flows but one that removes Tehran's most important external lever. The two powers agreed to an AI dialogue, but the 20-nation declaration for a global AI oversight body, issued days earlier with both Washington and Beijing absent, underscored that neither AI superpower wants multilateral constraints.

The day after the summit, China's ambassador to Japan warned Tokyo that 'the Taiwan issue is the core of China's core interests, and no external interference can be tolerated' — a sharp reminder that the trade truce does not extend to the security domain. Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi, who had suggested last November that Japan could intervene in a Taiwan contingency, received a detailed briefing from Trump on the summit and reaffirmed the US-Japan alliance as one of 'highest mutual trust.'
sections.whyItMatters: The summit lowered the temperature on the world's most consequential bilateral relationship and produced a measurable tariff cut, but the structural fault lines — Taiwan, Iran, AI supremacy — remain untouched. China's confirmation that it will not back Iran is the most strategically significant outcome: it isolates Tehran at the moment it most needs a patron.

sections.heading: Iran at the UN: Defiance on the Podium, a Seven-Day Deadline in the Back Channel
sections.body:
The Iran war framed every day of UN General Assembly week. It began with Trump telling world leaders that Iran faced a choice of 'potential greatness or obliteration,' saying he could 'annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly.' Minutes later, he confirmed that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a 'very good, very productive' three-hour meeting with Iranian leaders. The contradiction was the message.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian used his own UN address to reject Trump's ultimatum, telling the chamber Iran will 'never bow our head or bend the knee.' He held up photos of civilians he said were killed in US strikes — more than 175 people, two thirds of them children, according to Iranian authorities — on a school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd. The US denied striking Lamerd and says it is still investigating Minab.

Behind the rhetoric, a concrete proposal emerged. Iran formally presented a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt regional fighting, conveyed through Qatari mediators. Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters that 'if the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days.' Pezeshkian separately told reporters Tehran wants Washington to re-enter the memorandum of understanding by early November — explicitly tying the timeline to the US midterm elections.

Trump rejected the seven-day plan, calling it inadequate: 'They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly.' The rejection effectively closes the diplomatic window that opened with the June framework agreement. By Saturday, Araqchi said Tehran is still awaiting a formal US response, deliberately setting aside Trump's public remarks and waiting on mediators instead — keeping a thread of diplomacy alive, but with no new substance on the table.

The economic squeeze is visible. The UAE barred Iranian airlines, joining Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkmenistan in restricting access as US sanctions tighten around Iran's aviation sector. Oil prices slid about 2 percent on news of the Iranian proposal, reflecting market sensitivity to any de-escalation signal, before rebounding when Trump rejected it. European gas prices may stay elevated through winter as LNG disruptions persist.
sections.whyItMatters: Both sides are now bargaining through public statements and mediators rather than a working channel. The seven-day proposal is effectively a restatement of terms the US already rejected in June, so its rejection returns both sides to their starting positions — Hormuz closed, sanctions tightening, and the next move likely military rather than negotiated.

sections.heading: Ukraine's Largest Drone Strike on Moscow Meets a US Push for Trilateral Talks
sections.body:
The week opened with Ukraine launching its largest drone attack on the Moscow region since the war began. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital were shot down overnight, with at least two people killed and 20 injured. Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a 'key' Russian oil facility — a refinery supplying more than a third of the Moscow region's fuel, with petrol, diesel and aviation fuel going to Russia's military. Major airports including Sheremetyevo and Vnukovo imposed flight restrictions. The assault landed on the third day of Russia's parliamentary election, which Sobyanin described as an attempt to disrupt the vote.

Russia's election produced the expected supermajority for Putin's governing party, locking in an unambiguous political posture at home. Russia also warned that the new US sanctions law would harm Trump's peace efforts, signaling that the Kremlin sees the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict as interconnected bargaining fronts.

By midweek, the diplomatic gear shifted. The United States proposed a trilateral meeting with Ukrainian and Russian representatives in the UAE — the first direct three-party negotiation format of the war if it materializes. Zelensky confirmed the initiative on September 25. Putin told India Today that all proposals remain 'on the table' and that Russia is 'open to any serious settlement process,' a tonal shift from Moscow's recent rejection of interim arrangements. No date has been set.

Meanwhile, the battlefield ground on. Russian strikes killed seven people in Kyiv overnight, part of an escalating September campaign. An AFP analysis found a surge in Russian strikes on Kyiv's warehouse infrastructure. Reuters reported that Russian strikes shut down ArcelorMittal's electric steel plant — Ukraine's biggest steelmaker. In a notable break, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul held a surprise 20-minute meeting with Lavrov in New York, the first direct ministerial-level contact between Berlin and Moscow since the February 2022 invasion. Lavrov dismissed it as performative, saying Berlin could have simply read its own public statements.

Lavrov used his own UN address to accuse Europe of obstructing peace efforts, saying 'Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the Trump administration is interested.' The line is designed to exploit the emerging gap between Washington's desire for a deal and Europe's support for Kyiv — a gap Germany's outreach suggests Berlin is beginning to worry about.
sections.whyItMatters: A trilateral format, if it occurs, would be the first time all three principal parties sit at one table since the early 2022 Istanbul rounds. The fact that Washington is proposing it — rather than Kyiv or a neutral mediator — signals US interest in controlling the negotiation agenda. But Moscow's continued battlefield pressure and Lavrov's dismissal of German outreach suggest Putin sees little reason to compromise while his drones are hitting Kyiv's industrial base.

sections.heading: The Mecca Pact Moves From Declaration to Military Planning as the Houthis Bomb Riyadh
sections.body:
The Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence alliance, signed in August, moved from political declaration to operational military planning this week. Military chiefs from the three nations met in Riyadh on September 25 to finalize a joint defence mechanism, with Pakistan's Army Chief General Asim Munir meeting his Saudi and Turkish counterparts. The shift was preceded by a foreign ministers' meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA on September 24.

The operationalization came as Saudi Arabia absorbed continued Houthi attacks. The Houthis fired a wave of ballistic missiles and drones at Riyadh and Saudi oil facilities, with a reported strike on a fuel depot at Riyadh airport. Saudi Arabia said it shot down a missile aimed at the capital. The UK agreed to refuel Saudi jets to help counter the Houthi attacks — a concrete Western commitment to the Saudi war effort. Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi warned Pakistan and Turkiye against joining a Saudi-led escalation.

The NYT reported that the Trump administration prepared air attacks against the Houthis after renewed pleas from Riyadh — only for Trump to call them off at the last minute, even as soldiers were loading bombs onto aircraft. The administration has so far rebuffed Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's repeated requests for direct US military involvement.

In Yemen itself, Houthi forces are fighting Saudi-backed government troops for control of the Kahboub Mountains in Taiz and Lahj provinces — heights that overlook the Bab al-Mandeb strait and Mayyun Island. Renewed hostilities have killed at least 674 people and displaced more than 158,000. Houthi capture of the heights would let them cut the coast off from the remaining government-held south and give them effective control over one of the world's most critical shipping chokepoints.

Turkiye and Iraq separately agreed to a gradual transfer of Ankara's Bashiqa military base to Baghdad, removing a persistent source of friction and signaling Turkiye's willingness to formalize its security role in northern Iraq. Iraq's new Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi also vowed to disarm Iran-backed militias — the boldest rollback of Iranian influence in Baghdad in two decades.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca Pact is becoming a real military bloc — one that includes NATO member Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan, operates outside the US alliance framework, and is forming precisely as Washington declines to join the fight. If it produces deployed forces or integrated air defence, it creates a new security architecture in the Gulf that the US does not control. Trump's last-minute decision not to strike the Houthis reflects the administration's restraint, but the failure to act risks giving the Iran-aligned movement control over Bab al-Mandeb.

sections.heading: A US-Russia Deal to Gut Autonomous Weapons Safeguards Caps a Dark UN Session
sections.body:
As the 81st UN General Assembly closed, the Washington Post reported that US and Russian diplomats stripped key safeguards from a proposed UN framework on lethal autonomous weapons during closed-door negotiations in Geneva. The two delegations spent nearly 15 hours revising the document on the final day of talks held under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons — the UN's most advanced attempt to write rules for weapons that can identify, select and engage targets with limited or no human intervention.

The removed provisions included a requirement that humans review military targets selected by AI before an attack, standards that autonomous systems operate in a 'predictable' and 'reliable' manner, and language requiring ethical considerations. The talks were held behind closed doors after UN cameras were switched off and civil society observers were asked to leave, with each delegation fielding roughly 10 legal experts — nearly twice as many as most other countries. Human Rights Watch warned the weakened text could accelerate automated warfare with less accountability for civilian harm.

This came days after 20 countries and the EU issued a joint declaration calling for an international AI oversight body, led through the office of Finnish President Alexander Stubb. Signatories included Germany, South Africa, Canada, Australia, the UAE and Singapore. The US and China — the world's two leading AI powers — did not join. The declaration and the Geneva talks together describe a system in which the states with the most advanced AI capabilities are writing the rules bilaterally, or not at all.

Lavrov used the closing session to back India and Brazil for permanent Security Council seats while opposing them for Germany and Japan, who he said are 'on the path to militarism and revanchism.' The position deliberately splits the G4 coalition — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — converting a technical reform debate into an instrument of bloc politics.
sections.whyItMatters: A US-Russia joint deletion of human-review requirements means the two largest military powers have staked out a shared position against binding human control over AI weapons. The framework was the furthest any UN process had come on the issue; removing the safeguards leaves the field to whatever national rules the major powers choose to write. Lavrov's G4 split hardens the division at the heart of Security Council reform that has stalled enlargement for years.

sections.heading: Europe Under Diffuse Pressure: Sabotage, an Airspace Breach, and a Neutrality Vote
sections.body:
A pattern of Russian hybrid incidents accumulated along NATO's eastern flank. Poland said a fire at a Starlink satellite station — used in part to provide internet coverage to Ukraine — was sabotage. Poland separately accused a Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace for 42 seconds, forcing it to scramble fighter jets. Denmark warned of a rising Russian threat. A Croatian court approved the extradition of a Ukrainian man wanted in Germany over the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline bombings, though the ruling faces appeal; German prosecutors believe a Ukrainian state agency ordered the attack.

European leaders used the UNGA's final days to issue coordinated warnings about the near-term Russian threat, amid intelligence assessments suggesting Russia could test NATO's eastern flank within the next few years. The timing reflects growing concern that Washington's commitment to European defence may erode as US attention splits between the Iran war and the China relationship.

Switzerland voted on a referendum on Sunday to decide whether to enshrine a stricter definition of neutrality into its constitution. A 'yes' vote would effectively prevent Switzerland from imposing sanctions on Russia unless approved by the UN Security Council — where Moscow holds a veto — and would bar Bern from military cooperation with NATO unless Switzerland itself were attacked. Russia openly backed the initiative. Final polls showed nearly two-thirds of voters against, but the campaign exposed deep domestic divisions about Switzerland's Western alignment.

Germany's political fragility deepened through the week. Chancellor Merz's CDU slumped below the 5 percent threshold in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern — its worst result there ever — while the far-right AfD was on track to win the most votes in the state. Merz called the result 'a disaster' and faces speculation about a mid-term 'chancellor swap.' In Berlin, the CDU-led government was expected to be beaten by Die Linke.
sections.whyItMatters: A trail of sabotage, an airspace violation, and a pending pipeline-bombing extradition point to a steady, low-level Russian campaign of pressure that tests alliance resolve. The Swiss vote, even if it fails, signals that the neutralist impulse in Europe is politically viable — and that Russia sanctions remain domestically contested in at least one major European financial hub. Germany's electoral collapse adds political fragility to the security picture.

sections.heading: The Horn of Africa Slides Back Toward a 600,000-Death War
sections.body:
Fighting between Ethiopian federal forces and Tigrayan fighters intensified through the week, raising fears of a return to full-scale conflict. Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched operations in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced into a 'defensive war' following reported drone strikes. On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front announced an alliance with six other armed groups to remove the government in Addis Ababa. Ethiopian Airlines cancelled all flights to Tigray after local forces reportedly took over Mekelle's airport.

The army said it had repelled the attacks and inflicted casualties, while Tigrayan forces said they are in a 'full-blown war.' Both sides blame the other for restarting the conflict. The African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died in the 2020-2022 war, and the AU Commission chairperson called for immediate de-escalation. The US ambassador condemned the TPLF for launching 'a large-scale offensive' in what he called 'an unwinnable fight.'

The UN Security Council has not formally addressed the escalation, focusing instead on the Iran war and Ukraine diplomacy. The Horn of Africa's strategic position along the Red Sea corridor — the same waterway where Houthi attacks have disrupted global shipping — means instability in Ethiopia compounds the regional security picture, affecting Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia.
sections.whyItMatters: A second Ethiopia-Tigray war would destabilise a region already under strain from Sudan's civil war, Red Sea shipping disruptions, and great-power competition for basing rights. The international response has been minimal — a gap that regional actors, including the UAE and Egypt, may fill with their own agendas. This is a strategically consequential crisis being under-covered because global attention is fixed elsewhere.

sections.heading: Global Energy Adapts to the War: Saudi Exports Hit a War-High, Europe Scours for Jet Fuel
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia's crude exports surged to roughly 6 million barrels per day in September — the highest since the US-Iran war began about seven months ago — despite escalating fighting. September shipments rose nearly 80 percent from August's 3.4 million bpd average, according to trade-intelligence firm Kpler. The jump followed the shutdown of the East-West pipeline after a drone attack launched from Iraq, which forced the kingdom to reroute crude through the Strait of Hormuz after the US military secured a shipping corridor along the Omani coast. The seven-day average of oil exports through Hormuz stood at 13.2 million bpd on Wednesday, versus about 17 million bpd before the war.

The Iran war continues to reroute global energy supply chains. Europe faces a fourth-quarter jet fuel deficit of 510,000 barrels per day, consultancy Energy Aspects forecasts, with the continent turning to far-flung suppliers after the conflict cut off roughly half of its jet imports. South Korea boosted jet exports to Europe to a four-year high at 129,000 barrels per day in September. Europe has also been importing more jet fuel from Nigeria, the United States and Canada.

Separately, Washington's talk of a possible ban on diesel exports is widening US crude futures' discount to the global benchmark — another sign that war-driven fuel economics are now a domestic political problem in the United States. On the sidelines of the UN, Trump's Board of Peace announced a $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan spread across 66 programmes over six months, but acknowledged that only $280 million of $18 billion pledged has been delivered, with full reconstruction estimated at $71.4 billion over a decade.
sections.whyItMatters: Gulf producers are regaining confidence in the Hormuz corridor even as their own infrastructure is under attack — bullish for global supply and a reason Brent pulled back after spiking near $110. But the structural disruption is durable: Europe is now importing jet fuel from Asia and the Americas at record distances, and a US diesel export ban would add another layer of government intervention in energy markets that are already warped by war.

bottomLine: This was a week of diplomatic choreography that closed every door it opened. The Trump-Xi summit produced a trade truce extension and $30 billion in tariff cuts but no movement on Iran, Taiwan, or AI — though China's confirmation that it will not back Tehran is the most strategically significant outcome, isolating Iran at the moment it most needs a patron. Iran's seven-day Hormuz proposal was rejected by Trump, returning both sides to their starting positions with the strait closed and the next move likely military. Washington proposed the first trilateral Ukraine-Russia talks in the UAE, and Putin says he is 'open' — but his drones are still hitting Kyiv's industrial base and Lavrov dismissed Germany's first ministerial outreach in four years as empty theater. The Mecca Pact moved from signature to military planning as the Houthis bombed Riyadh and Trump called off US strikes at the last minute. A US-Russia deal gutted the UN's autonomous weapons safeguards, Lavrov split the G4 by backing India and Brazil while rejecting Germany and Japan, and Ethiopia slid back toward a war that killed 600,000. The common thread: the world's major powers are managing crises in parallel rather than resolving them, and the multilateral system is being shaped around the interests of its strongest members — not by its rules.
sources: BBC, Al Jazeera, The New York Times, Reuters, AFP, Xinhua, Politico, The Guardian, Japan Times, Straits Times, Dawn, Gulf News, Al Arabiya, Iran International, IRNA, Anadolu Agency, CNBC, Washington Post, IANS, Hindustan Times, Times of India, Financial Express, Business Today, South China Morning Post, Energy Aspects, Kpler, Goldman Sachs, Human Rights Watch
